[[File:Rodolfo Rodolfo.jpg|thumb|Rodolfo Bonifacio at INFN, Frascati, June 2012]]

'''Rodolfo Bonifacio''' ([[Messina]], 24 February 1940 – [[Rome]], 1 November 2016)<ref>{{Cite web |date=6 December 2016 |title=Rodolfo Bonifacio |url=https://pubs.aip.org/physicstoday/online/10624/Rodolfo-Bonifacio |access-date=2023-12-27 |website=Physics Today}}</ref> was an Italian physicist, Professor Emeritus at [[University of Milan]], who made significant contributions to [[laser physics]] and [[quantum optics]].

== Education and career ==
Bonifacio studied in Milan, graduating with Piero Caldirola in 1964. He was a postdoctoral student at [[Harvard University]] with [[Roy J. Glauber|Roy Glauber]]. Afterwards he was a professor in Milan. He was also in the Milan section of the [[Istituto Nazionale di Fisica Nucleare|Istituto Nazionale di Fisica Nucleare (INFN)]].

He has been a visiting professor and visiting scientist at [[Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory]], [[Stanford Linear Accelerator Center]], and [[Brookhaven National Laboratory]].

== Research ==
As part of their investigation of the nonlinear interaction of an electromagnetic pulse with an ensemble of two-level atoms, he and [[Tito Arecchi]] independently derived the equations known as [[Maxwell–Bloch equations|Maxwell-Bloch equations]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Arecchi |first1=F. |last2=Bonifacio |first2=R. |date=1965 |title=Theory of optical maser amplifiers |journal=IEEE Journal of Quantum Electronics |language=en |volume=1 |issue=4 |pages=169–178 |doi=10.1109/JQE.1965.1072212 |bibcode=1965IJQE....1..169A |issn=0018-9197}}</ref> In 1970, with Paolo Schwendimann and Fritz Haake, he developed a classical and quantum theory of [[Spontaneous emission|cooperative spontaneous emission]]<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Bonifacio |first1=R. |last2=Gronchi |first2=M. |date=1 June 1971 |title=An analytical result about co-operative spontaneous emission |journal=Lettere al Nuovo Cimento (1971–1985) |language=en |volume=1 |issue=26 |pages=1105–1108 |doi=10.1007/BF02770373 |s2cid=124354237 |issn=1827-613X}}</ref> and coined the name ''superfluorescence''.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Bonifacio |first1=R. |last2=Lugiato |first2=L. A. |date=1 May 1975 |title=Cooperative radiation processes in two-level systems: Superfluorescence |journal=Physical Review A |volume=11 |issue=5 |pages=1507–1521 |doi=10.1103/physreva.11.1507 |bibcode=1975PhRvA..11.1507B |issn=0556-2791}}</ref> With [[Luigi Lugiato]] he later described oscillating superfluorescence, which was confirmed experimentally.<ref>{{Citation |last1=Vrehen |first1=Q. H. F. |chapter=Superfluorescence Experiments |date=1982 |title=Dissipative Systems in Quantum Optics: Resonance Fluorescence, Optical Bistability, Superfluorescence |pages=111–147 |editor-last=Bonifacio |editor-first=Rodolfo  |series=Topics in Current Physics |place=Berlin, Heidelberg |publisher=Springer |language=en |doi=10.1007/978-3-642-81717-5_6 |isbn=978-3-642-81717-5 |last2=Gibbs |first2=H. M.|volume=27 }}</ref> In addition, with Lugiato he developed a molecular field theory of [[optical bistability]]<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Bonifacio |first1=R. |last2=Lugiato |first2=L. A. |date=1 September 1978 |title=Optical bistability and cooperative effects in resonance fluorescence |url=https://link.aps.org/doi/10.1103/PhysRevA.18.1129 |journal=Physical Review A |volume=18 |issue=3 |pages=1129–1144 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevA.18.1129|bibcode=1978PhRvA..18.1129B |url-access=subscription }}</ref> with a description of photon statistics and they developed an exact theory of optical bistability in a ring resonator with later experimentally confirmed prediction of optical self-pulsing.

In 1982 he described a model of the [[Free-electron laser|free electron laser (FEL)]] with Federico Casagrande and [[Giulio Casati]]. They predicted a first-order phase transition to laser operation for critical values of the magnetic wiggler field and electron density.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Bonifacio |first1=R. |last2=Casagrande |first2=F. |last3=Casati |first3=G. |date=1 January 1982 |title=Cooperative and chaotic transition of a free electron laser Hamiltonian model |journal=Optics Communications |volume=40 |issue=3 |pages=219–223 |doi=10.1016/0030-4018(82)90265-6 |bibcode=1982OptCo..40..219B |issn=0030-4018}}</ref>

In the 1990s he studied the interaction of cold atomic gases with light<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Robb |first1=G. R. M. |last2=Piovella |first2=N. |last3=Ferraro |first3=A. |last4=Bonifacio |first4=R. |last5=Courteille |first5=Ph. W. |last6=Zimmermann |first6=C. |date=27 April 2004 |title=Collective atomic recoil lasing including friction and diffusion effects |url=https://link.aps.org/doi/10.1103/PhysRevA.69.041403 |journal=Physical Review A |volume=69 |issue=4 |article-number=041403 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevA.69.041403|arxiv=quant-ph/0311012 |bibcode=2004PhRvA..69d1403R |hdl=2434/751997 |s2cid=56065335 }}</ref> and developed the theory of the Collective Atomic Recoil Laser<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Bonifacio |first1=R. |last2=De Salvo |first2=L. |date=1 March 1994 |title=Collective atomic recoil laser (CARL) optical gain without inversion by collective atomic recoil and self-bunching of two-level atoms |journal=Nuclear Instruments and Methods in Physics Research Section A: Accelerators, Spectrometers, Detectors and Associated Equipment |volume=341 |issue=1 |pages=360–362 |doi=10.1016/0168-9002(94)90382-4 |bibcode=1994NIMPA.341..360B |issn=0168-9002}}</ref> (CARL, 1994), in which both internal atomic states and the movement of atoms play a role (so that he experiences both the theory of conventional lasers and FEL). This has been observed as superradiant Rayleigh scattering<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Bonifacio |first1=R. |last2=Cataliotti |first2=F. S. |last3=Cola |first3=M. |last4=Fallani |first4=L. |last5=Fort |first5=C. |last6=Piovella |first6=N. |last7=Inguscio |first7=M. |date=March 2004 |title=Superradiant light scattering from a moving Bose-Einstein condensate |journal=Optics Communications |volume=233 |issue=1–3 |pages=155–160 |doi=10.1016/j.optcom.2004.01.027|arxiv=cond-mat/0306500 |bibcode=2004OptCo.233..155B |s2cid=34661014 }}</ref> (SRyS) in both ordinary cold atomic gases and [[Bose Einstein condensate|Bose-Einstein condensate]] (BEC). The latter suggested an extension of the CARL model, which also included the atomic recoil during photon emission, which led Bonifacio to investigate a possible new regime of FEL called Quantum FEL (QFEL)<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Robb |first1=G. R. M. |last2=Bonifacio |first2=R. |date=1 July 2012 |title=Coherent and spontaneous emission in the quantum free electron laser |journal=Physics of Plasmas |volume=19 |issue=7 |article-number=073101 |doi=10.1063/1.4729337 |bibcode=2012PhPl...19g3101R |issn=1070-664X}}</ref> in the 2000s, building on the work of [[Giuliano Preparata]] at the end of the 2000s 1980s. He saw this as a possible compact source for coherent gamma radiation.

He also dealt with the nature and quantization of time.<ref>{{Citation |title=What is Time? – Rodolfo Bonifacio | date=28 June 2016 |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZzKO7Tfmpmg |access-date=2023-11-28 |language=en}}

General Seminar – Scientific Event 15 June 2016, Auditorium B. Touschek INFN – Laboratori Nazionali di Frascati</ref>

In 1987 he received the [[Albert A. Michelson Medal]] from the [[Franklin Institute]] with Luigi A. Lugiato and in 1994 the [[Einstein Prize for Laser Science|Einstein Medal from the Society for Quantum Optics and Quantum Electronics]].

An article published in [[Nature (journal)|Nature]] in 2015 with the title ''Due credit for Maxwell–Bloch equations''<ref>{{Cite journal |last=McNeil |first=Brian |date=2015 |title=Due credit for Maxwell–Bloch equations |journal=Nature |language=en |volume=9 |issue=4 |page=207 |doi=10.1038/nphoton.2015.44 |issn=1749-4885|doi-access=free |bibcode=2015NaPho...9..207M }}</ref> authored by Brian McNeil<ref>{{Cite web |title=Dr Brian McNeil {{!}} University of Strathclyde |url=https://www.strath.ac.uk/staff/mcneilbriandr/ |access-date=2023-11-28 |website=www.strath.ac.uk |language=en}}</ref> suggests that ''"These coupled equations were not actually derived by Maxwell and Bloch, but instead can be traced back to a little cited (given its significance) publication by Tito Arecchi and Rodolfo Bonifacio''".
